# NexusPiercer round-trip fidelity guarantee

**What a document loses, and does not lose, when NexusPiercer flattens and reconstructs it.**

Measured, not asserted. Every number and every row below is generated from the corpus manifest
recorded on 2026-08-11, and the corpus is executed on every build.

| | count |
| --- | ---: |
| documents in the corpus | 156 |
| reproduce the source exactly (`LOSSLESS`) | 51 |
| lose something, by accepted design (`ACCEPTED_LOSS`) | 23 |
| lose something, wrongly (`DEFECT`) | 82 |
| measured under non-default configuration | 50 |
| `LOSSLESS` rows that do **not** hold through the default reconstruction entry point | 3 |
| `LOSSLESS` rows the **published recipe on this page** cannot reproduce | 1 |
| rows for which no published recipe exists (schema-only paths) | 44 |
| rows the **published recipe** cannot reproduce at all | 24 |

**23 + 82 = 105 of 156 documents do not survive a round trip.** That ratio is the headline fact about
this library. It is high because the corpus was built adversarially - it hunts for the shapes that
break rather than sampling shapes at random - but every one of those rows is a shape real data has.

## 1. Read this before you depend on the library

Stated without softening, because the point of the list is that you meet these here rather than in
production. Each item names the fixtures that hold it in place; if the behaviour is ever repaired,
those fixtures fail and the item has to be withdrawn from this page.

**1. An array of objects does not survive the round trip.**

This is the most common shape in real data - order line items, event attachments, CDC row images - and under default configuration it comes back wrong. Elements are duplicated, elements are deleted, or the array is rebuilt as an object keyed by index. A two-element array of objects at the document root does round-trip, and so does any array whose path is named explicitly to JsonReconstructor.arrayPaths(...) with inferArraysFromValues(false); nothing else in this corpus does. Treat arrayPaths as mandatory, not optional.

**2. An array of scalars turns its parent object into an array.**

A list of strings one level below the root does not come back as a list of strings inside an object: the containing object itself is reconstructed as a JSON array. At the document root an array of scalars never reconstructs at all.

<sub>Pinned by: `nested-array-of-scalars`, `order-top-level-tags-array`, `top-level-array-of-scalars`, `array-of-arrays-with-empty-inner`</sub>

**3. An empty object, an empty array and an explicit null are the same value afterwards.**

{} and [] and null all flatten to null and all reconstruct as null. Three distinct authored values arrive as one. If your schema distinguishes "no items" from "field not set", this library cannot carry that distinction. The nesting DEPTH of an empty chain is preserved, which means you get keys back with no leaves under them.

<sub>Pinned by: `vd-empty-containers-end-to-end`, `empty-containers-at-depth`, `empty-cart`, `empty-chains-yield-keys-with-zero-leaves`</sub>

**4. A non-finite number is indistinguishable afterwards from a string of the same text.**

Two separate facts, split because only one of them was previously backed by a fixture. (a) A literal that overflows a double during PARSING becomes the text "Infinity" - vd-exponent-overflow-and-underflow records a genuine Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY going through the flattener's isInfinite branch. (b) A non-finite Double handed to flatten() by a Spark Row is byte-identical afterwards to a user string of the same text - vd-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text. JSON has no NaN literal, so (b) was unassertable until the typed input hatch existed.

<sub>Pinned by: `vd-exponent-overflow-and-underflow`, `vd-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text`</sub>

**5. An integer past Long.MAX_VALUE stops being a number and becomes a quoted string.**

The digits survive exactly - nothing is truncated and no value wraps negative, which an earlier version of this library did do - but the JSON type changes from number to string. Anything downstream that type-checks before parsing will reject it.

<sub>Pinned by: `vd-integer-past-long`, `financial-transaction-huge-minor-units`</sub>

**6. Declared decimal scale is destroyed, and the flag that claims to prevent that cannot fire on the JSON stack.**

37.7740 comes back as 37.774; an 18-digit FX rate is rounded to a double. preserveBigDecimalPrecision keeps exact text when you hand MapFlattener a real BigDecimal, but the JSON stack parses fractional numbers to Double before the flattener ever runs, so on that stack the flag is inert. Do not carry money through this library as a JSON number.

**7. Field names made of underscores collide with the library's internal markers and are silently deleted.**

A field named ___ is dropped outright - no exception, no warning, no null placeholder (NP-022). The whole __*__ namespace is swallowed, including entire subtrees beneath it, which takes out the __meta__ and __type__ headers that event envelopes routinely carry. A field named __isArray__ converts its parent object into a JSON array. An empty-string key is renamed to empty_key and overwrites any real sibling of that name.

**8. Anything whose serialised text starts with a bracket is turned into an array.**

The collision class is wider than a string that merely looks like an array, and it is two classes rather than one. THREE members are BYTE-IDENTICAL and two pair invariants assert it: a genuine array, a scalar string containing array text, and a byte[] all flatten to exactly S:[1,2,3] - the last of them with no string and no array anywhere in the input. Object[] and Set belong to the class only in the weaker sense that they too become bracket-leading strings and retype their parent as a list; they carry different element values, so they are pinned by vd-object-array-and-set-become-array-text's own recording and by no byte-equality pair. Whichever one you fed in, the parent object is retyped as an array on the way back. This previously read "all flatten to the same bracket-leading value", which a reader of the neighbouring byte-identity invariant would have taken for byte identity of all five.

**9. ArraySerializationFormat.COMMA_SEPARATED invents arrays out of ordinary strings.**

A comma anywhere inside a scalar string - a product description, an address - makes that string reconstruct as an array. Element types are coerced, and an empty or trailing-null element is lost entirely rather than merely retyped. This format is not safe for free text.

**10. The naming strategies restructure the document rather than only renaming fields.**

SNAKE_CASE injects unescaped separator characters, which turns a flat scalar field into a nested object on the way back. The case-collision disambiguator emits an unescaped _2 that the decoder reads as another level of nesting. The same field name is sanitised differently at the root than deeper down, so one name yields two column names. UPPER_CASE is the one strategy that renames without damaging the encoding.

**11. maxDepth, maxArraySize and maxMapSize discard data with no marker, no warning and no exception.**

Past maxDepth the subtree is replaced by its JSON text, which is indistinguishable from a user string that happens to contain that text - the corpus pins that collision as a pair invariant. Past maxArraySize the extra elements are gone. Past maxMapSize the trailing fields are gone. maxArraySize=1 does not shorten the array, it changes the reconstructed type from array to object, so a resource bound silently rewrites your schema. maxDepth(0) is the one bound that fails closed, at configuration time.

Absent-key versus present-null is preserved by default and is one of the guarantees this corpus does make - but turning preserveNulls off voids it silently, and inside an array of objects a field missing from one element comes back as an explicit null on that element.

**13. A mixed-type array loses elements or leaks an internal sentinel into your data.**

With objects before the scalars the object elements are silently deleted. With scalars first the flattener's internal marker appears in the reconstructed document as if it were a value.

**14. An Avro union takes the first branch that will accept the value and coerces to it.**

A string branch listed before int turns every value in that field into text. [long, double] truncates a fractional value to an integer. For a union of records, the first branch sharing any field name wins and the remaining data is dropped. A nullable string whose value is the literal text "null" comes back as an actual null.

**15. One null element destroys an entire Avro array of records.**

A single null inside an array of records annihilates the whole array, and one null nested record erases the nested records of every other element in that array.

**16. Avro schema flattening erases logical types, field defaults, and enum and fixed identity.**

Every logical type on a field inside an array becomes an untyped STRING column. Field defaults are gone from the reconstructed schema. A fixed-backed decimal loses precision and scale and arrives as uninterpretable bytes. reconstructOriginalSchema never reads its flattenedSchema argument at all - it replays definitions stored during the forward pass, so it will reproduce an original schema even when the flattened schema has thrown the information away. The flattened SCHEMA and the flattened ROWS disagree on column names for any field containing an underscore.

**17. Two controls do not do what their names say.**

useArrayBoundarySeparator marks no array boundaries; it is a global rename of the separator from _ to __, and switching it on collapses __ inside field names and manufactures collisions that did not exist. strictKeyValidation performs no validation and rejects nothing; it silently rewrites names, and three distinct names can fold into one column.

**18. Three settings are wired, documented, readable - and cannot change the output.** *(a setting that does nothing, not a data loss)*

JsonReconstructor.maxDepth and MapFlattener.preserveBigDecimalPrecision on the JSON stack were the first two, and MapFlattener.detectCircularReferences is the third: it has no effect on a self-referential List, because the visit-stack calls exist only on the object path. Each is proven inert by a probe that measures the two settings producing byte-identical output. A FOURTH was listed here until now - FlattenOptions.inheritDoc, which was read nowhere in src/main - and it has been repaired rather than merely documented: it is now honoured, its probe expects the two settings to DIFFER, and its row is published LOSSLESS as enriched-inheritdoc-false-reports-declared-only-docs.

<sub>Pinned by: `reconstructor-maxdepth-is-a-dead-control`, `vd-preserve-bigdecimal-flag-inert`, `circular-list-reference-escapes-the-guard`</sub>

**19. reconstruct() returns an Avro record that cannot be written.**

AvroReconstructor has two data entry points and they do not agree. reconstructToMap returns a Map and is what the LOSSLESS Avro rows are about. reconstruct returns a GenericRecord, and it rebuilds only the ROOT record: every nested record, array element and map value is left as the raw LinkedHashMap the map-building step produced. The builder validates nullability and nothing else, so build() succeeds, the object looks correct in a debugger, GenericData.validate returns false and writing it throws ClassCastException in an executor. An empty flattened map makes the two entry points disagree outright: one returns a partial record, the other throws. A SECOND, INDEPENDENT CAUSE OF THE SAME FAILURE, measured 2026-08-17 and tracked as BL-012 / SECURITY.md recon/NP-023: even the ROOT record fails validate when the schema has a defaulted ENUM field that is absent from the input, at the SHIPPED DEFAULT configuration and with no nesting involved. useSchemaDefaults(true) - the default - sets field.defaultVal() itself, which routes through JacksonUtils.toObject and yields a plain java.lang.String for an enum default (byte[] for FIXED/BYTES, LinkedHashMap for a record-typed default), and GenericRecordBuilder.set does not type-check. useSchemaDefaults(false) reconstructs it correctly, so the default is the broken setting. This is not repaired here because the repair changes default-configuration output and would move Avro fixtures; it is disclosed rather than hidden.

<sub>Pinned by: `avro-generic-record-is-not-a-valid-datum`, `avro-array-of-records-datum-unwritable`, `avro-map-of-records-datum-unwritable`, `avro-empty-datum-cannot-build-a-record`</sub>

**20. A self-referential schema kills the task rather than failing the record.**

AvroSchemaFlattener walks a schema with neither a visited set nor an open-type set, so a record containing itself exhausts the JVM stack in the first pass. The failure is a StackOverflowError, an Error, so ordinary per-record error handling does not catch it and the Spark task dies. EnrichedSchemaFlattener refuses the same schema with a typed RecursiveSchemaException naming the cycle, which is the correct behaviour and is why that pair is the argument for the new API.

<sub>Pinned by: `avro-recursive-schema-stack-overflows`, `enriched-recursive-schema-fails-typed`</sub>

**21. The cached schema factory identifies a schema by its name, not its content.**

getFlattenedSchema(Schema) memoises in a process-wide static map keyed on the schema's full name plus two flags. Flatten two versions of the same named record in one JVM and the second silently receives the first's columns, and the instance's record definitions are left describing the first, so the schema inverse replays it too. In a long-lived executor a registry version bump is discarded for the JVM lifetime.

<sub>Pinned by: `avro-schema-cache-serves-a-stale-flattened-schema`</sub>

**22. The enriched schema API names columns your rows do not have, and its defaults are deliberately not the flattener it replaces.**

Under its default collision policy EnrichedSchemaFlattener emits field names verbatim while MapFlattener escapes them, so the StructType it describes and the rows the library produces disagree on every field containing the separator. Its defaults also differ from GAvroSchemaFlattener's names on two independent axes - escaping, and the array-boundary marker - and that is now a deliberate choice rather than a broken promise: the parity claim has been withdrawn from the defaults, and FlattenOptions.gAvroParity() reproduces GAvro's names for callers migrating, at the cost of emitting backslashes that are illegal in Avro and SQL identifiers. PARITY IS SCOPED, NOT UNCONDITIONAL, and the page used to say otherwise: it holds for record-rooted schemas that avoid a union with more than one non-null branch, an array of arrays of records, depth past 50, and a non-record root. On the first two a whole subtree collapses to one leaf - GAvro yields payload_k and grid_v where the parity preset yields payload and grid - so the column is missing rather than renamed and no configuration reaches it; both are now measured. The depth divergence is measured nowhere and is prose on the factory's javadoc. The ESCAPE policy is INJECTIVE but NOT DECODABLE: the array-boundary marker is emitted outside the escaped alphabet, so splitting a rendered name yields a phantom empty segment at every boundary - use pathSegments() and arrayBoundaries(), never the name. NO TWO EMITTED COLUMNS SHARE A FLATTENED NAME, under either policy and for injected columns as well as source ones: a boundary marker an ordinary field name can spell is refused, and so is a name supplied through injectField() that another column already holds. THREE WARNINGS THAT USED TO STAND HERE HAVE BEEN REPAIRED and their rows are now LOSSLESS: stream() no longer discards configured column injections that flatten() honours, a producer property whose name collides with an Avro structural attribute at a different position is no longer dropped, and inheritDoc(false) no longer returns inherited documentation. TWO MORE OUTPUT-SIDE GUARDS WERE REPAIRED THAT NO WARNING EVER STOOD FOR, because no fixture could see them: injectField() bypassed the collision guard under both policies, so an injected name equal to a source column's returned two columns of one name even under FAIL, and maxFields bounded only the leaves the traversal visited, so maxFields(2) with two injections returned four columns. The first now has a row of its own; the second is covered by unit test only, because the corpus has no assert mode that can see a field-count ceiling.

**23. Every Java value that is not a String, Number or Boolean leaves this library as a String.**

Stack A's declared input is Map<String,Object> and Spark supplies Date, Instant, UUID, enum constants, byte[], Object[], Set and non-String map keys through it. All of them are erased, none is marked, and the library offers no inverse. java.util.Date is worse than erased: it is flattened via Date.toString(), which formats through the JVM default timezone, so the flattened value is not a function of its input and two executors in different regions emit different data. A non-String map key is stringified and, on collision, renamed to a field name nobody wrote.

<sub>Pinned by: `vd-java-native-temporal-and-identity`, `vd-java-date-is-not-a-function-of-its-input`, `non-string-map-keys-collide-and-are-disambiguated`</sub>

**24. The cycle guard marks Map cycles and misses List cycles.**

detectCircularReferences defaults on and works: a self-referential Map is cut with an explicit marker rather than hanging. It does nothing for a self-referential List, because the visit-stack calls exist only on the object path, so the list case is bounded by maxDepth alone and emits nested brackets around a JDK toString artefact with no marker at all. Neither marker is escaped, so both are aliasable by data a user could legitimately have authored.

**25. The code on this page was, until now, free text that nothing compiled and nothing ran.**

Every stack recipe published here is now the body of a compiled method, extracted from source and asserted byte-identical, and each one is executed against a corpus row and compared to that row's recording. That gate found two live faults in what this page previously published: the JSON recipe could not compile at all, because JsonFlattener's constructor is private and, at 2.0.0, no public member returned the type (2.1.0's Builder.buildFlattener() has since changed that, but the recipe was already corrected and is unaffected); and the Avro recipe named a statically cached factory that no measurement in the corpus had ever executed and that returns another schema's columns when a name repeats. EVERY row publishes holdsUnderPublishedRecipe - not a third of them - and the number that say NO is the derived figure in the summary table and in section 5. ## 2. What round-trip fidelity means here

THIS FILE IS THE CONTRACT. For every fixture below it states what a JSON or Avro document loses, or does not lose, when it is flattened and reconstructed. A consumer can read a line here and rely on it.

The repository cannot change any of these behaviours quietly. Each fixture file carries the exact recorded rendering of its flattened intermediate and its reconstructed document, and RoundTripFidelityCorpusTest asserts both. Changing behaviour - including FIXING a defect - makes a recording stale and turns the build red until someone updates this manifest on purpose. That is the intended cost: the published guarantee may not drift by accident.

The oracle is strict recursive equality with runtime types attached, not JsonReconstructor verify(), which treats String and Number as compatible and compares doubles with a 1e-6 tolerance and would report several of these fixtures as PERFECT.

Concretely, two documents count as equal only when every scalar has the same runtime type, every
list has the same length and order, every key set matches, and an absent key is distinct from a
present null. `1`, `1L` and `"1"` are three different values; `-0.0` is distinct from `0.0`;
`37.7740` is distinct from `37.774`.

## 3. The stacks this applies to

A fixture declared `BOTH` is measured on Stack A and Stack B independently and must satisfy both.

### Stack A - Map level  <sub>`MAP`</sub>

```java
MapFlattener f = MapFlattener.builder().build();
Map<String, Object> flat = f.flatten(sourceMap);
Map<String, Object> back = JsonReconstructor.quickReconstruct(flat);
// lossless means back.equals(sourceMap)
```

The source is an in-memory Java Map. Anything a JSON parser would have destroyed before flatten() was called is already absent from the source AND from the result, so this stack is structurally blind to parse-time loss. Fixtures that measure parse-time loss are declared JSON-only for that reason. SECOND, LARGER CAVEAT: until the typed javaInput hatch existed, every MAP row's source was produced by a JSON parser, so this stack exercised only the JSON value domain - String, Boolean, Integer, Long, Double, BigInteger, List, Map, null - which is a strict subset of what flatten(Map<String,Object>) accepts. Spark supplies Date, Instant, UUID, enums, byte[], Object[], Set and non-String keys through the same signature, and all of them are erased; see the java-value-domain warning. Nine LOSSLESS MAP rows read differently once that is stated.

### Stack B - JSON level  <sub>`JSON`</sub>

```java
Map<String, Object> flat = JsonFlattener.create().from(jsonString).toMap();
String back = JsonReconstructor.builder().build().reconstructToJson(flat);
// lossless means back is semantically equal to jsonString
```

The source is JSON text. Jackson parses it before the flattener runs, so this stack sees parse-time loss - declared decimal scale, exponent overflow - that Stack A cannot see. The corpus compares the two documents with BigDecimal-exact parsing on both sides: comparing the raw text would fail on 1e2 versus 100.0, and comparing with a default mapper would collapse both sides to the same Double and hide the money loss. TWO DISCLOSURES ADDED AFTER THE RECIPE WAS FIRST COMPILED. (1) HISTORICAL, and no longer true as of 2.1.0. The recipe published here once declared a JsonFlattener variable, which could not compile at 2.0.0: the class's only constructor is private, and create(), both with(...) overloads and Builder.build() all returned FluentOperation, so no public member returned the type and flattenToMap, flattenToJson and flattenMapToJson were unreachable from outside the package. (Note the fourth factory, builder(), returned Builder, not FluentOperation - an earlier wording of this note said "all four factories return FluentOperation", which was wrong on its own terms.) 2.1.0 added Builder.buildFlattener(), which IS a public member returning JsonFlattener, so those three methods are now reachable and the compile obstacle is gone. The recipe below is unchanged regardless, because it reaches the same code: FluentOperation.from(String) delegates to flattenToMap. (2) Do NOT generalise that: from(Map) and from(JsonNode) bypass flattenToMap entirely and call the map flattener directly, so "FluentOperation always routes through flattenToMap" is false. (3) A CAVEAT ON THE NEWLY REACHABLE ENGINE METHODS, added with them: flattenToJson and flattenMapToJson take their own explicit pretty argument and select a mapper from it, so JsonFlattenerConfig.usePrettyPrint does not reach them; and charset, bufferSize, failOnError, preserveNulls and sortKeys are read nowhere in src/main at all. Measured, not inferred - see BL-015 and the inertness probe in JsonFlattenerReusableEngineTest.

### Stack C - Avro  <sub>`AVRO`</sub>

```java
AvroSchemaFlattener.clearCache();
AvroSchemaFlattener sf = new AvroSchemaFlattener(false, true);
// getFlattenedSchemaNoCache, NOT getFlattenedSchema: the cached factory keys on the
// schema's full name and returns another schema's columns when the name repeats.
// flatSchema is the Spark-facing COLUMN LAYOUT - build your StructType from it.
// Reconstruction takes the ORIGINAL schema, not this one.
Schema flatSchema = sf.getFlattenedSchemaNoCache(schema);
Map<String, Object> flat = MapFlattener.builder().build().flatten(datum);
Map<String, Object> back = AvroReconstructor.builder().build().reconstructToMap(flat, schema);
```

Two separate things are measured and they do not agree with each other: the DATA path (flatten a datum, reconstruct it against the writer schema) and the SCHEMA path (flatten a schema, then ask reconstructOriginalSchema to invert it). The schema inverse replays definitions captured during the forward pass rather than reading the flattened schema, so it reproduces the original even when the flattened schema has discarded the information. The corpus therefore never accepts the inverse alone as a verdict; it conjoins it with direct checks on what the flattened schema still carries. THREE DISCLOSURES. (1) The DATA path has TWO entry points and they do not agree: reconstructToMap returns a Map and is what every DATA row measures, while reconstruct returns a GenericRecord whose nested records are raw maps - it fails GenericData.validate and throws on a binary encode. Rows asserting DATUM measure that second entry point, and three LOSSLESS Map rows are qualified accordingly. (2) Every SCHEMA, KEYSET and enriched row is measured through getFlattenedSchemaNoCache; the recipe above says so explicitly because the previously published recipe named the statically CACHED getFlattenedSchema(Schema), which no row had ever executed. Exactly one row, avro-schema-cache-serves-a-stale-flattened-schema, exercises the cached factory, and it shows the cache keying on the schema's full name and serving another version's columns. (3) The enriched schema API (EnrichedSchemaFlattener.flatten and .stream, measured by the ENRICHED_KEYSET and ENRICHED_METADATA modes) has no inverse, so "fidelity" for the schema family means agreement between producers and encode/decode reversibility - never flatten-then-rebuild. No row in that family is evidence that data flattened under an enriched StructType comes back.

### Stack C - Avro, schema inverse  <sub>`AVRO_SCHEMA`</sub>

```java
AvroSchemaFlattener.clearCache();
AvroSchemaFlattener sf = new AvroSchemaFlattener(false, true);
Schema flatSchema = sf.getFlattenedSchemaNoCache(schema);
Schema original = sf.reconstructOriginalSchema(flatSchema);
```

Six Avro rows are measured on this path and until now the manifest published no recipe for it at all. Read the result with the same warning the data note carries: reconstructOriginalSchema REPLAYS record definitions captured during the forward pass rather than reading the flattened schema, so it reproduces the original even when the flattened schema has discarded the information, and it throws outright if the forward pass was served from the cache. The KEYSET path (avro-underscore-field-name-column-divergence) still has no published recipe; that is disclosed here rather than folded into this one.

## 4. What the three classifications mean

### `LOSSLESS` - 51 documents

The round trip reproduces the source exactly under the corpus oracle: identical runtime types for every scalar, identical list lengths and order, identical key sets, and absent-vs-present-null preserved. The harness asserts equality against the source AND against the recorded rendering.

> **Repair status.** Not a repair category. These rows are the guarantee. They may not silently get worse; a change here fails the build.

### `ACCEPTED_LOSS` - 23 documents

The round trip does NOT reproduce the source, the loss is understood, bounded, and judged the right trade. The harness asserts the loss is still present AND that its exact shape matches the recording, so the deal cannot silently get worse - or silently get better without someone updating this file.

> **Repair status.** ACCEPTED DESIGN LIMIT. Not scheduled for repair. The loss is understood and bounded, and the corpus pins its exact shape so it cannot silently widen. If one of these is unacceptable for your data, the answer is not to wait for a fix - it is to avoid the shape or configure around it.

### `DEFECT` - 82 documents

The round trip does NOT reproduce the source and the loss is wrong. The harness asserts the exact wrong output. Fixing the defect makes the recorded output stale and the test FAILS - deliberately. A fix must land together with a manifest update, because the guarantee published to consumers changes at that moment.

> **Repair status.** UNDER ACTIVE REPAIR. The behaviour is wrong, not merely limited. The corpus records the exact wrong output that comes out today, so the day a defect is repaired the recording goes stale and the build turns red on purpose - a fix has to land together with a rewrite of this contract, because what is promised to consumers changes at that moment. Do not read a DEFECT row as a fixed date; read it as a hazard that is currently live.

## 5. Which rows are only true under a non-default configuration

Every row in the table below was measured under a stated configuration. 50 of 156 rows
turn some knob away from its default, and the `config` column says which.

The sharper question is whether a row still describes what happens through the library's *default*
reconstruction entry point - `JsonReconstructor.quickReconstruct`, `quickReconstructToJson`, or a
default-built `AvroReconstructor`. The harness reconstructs a second time that way and compares, and the
`defaults` column publishes the answer. `NOT_APPLICABLE` means the row reconstructs no data at all -
the Avro schema-only rows.

The sharpest question of the three is the `recipe` column: does the row still hold when you run the
code block published in section 3 verbatim? That is strictly stronger than the `defaults` column, which
only re-reconstructs a map the row's own flattener already produced and is therefore blind to any
divergence the FLATTENER creates. Every recipe on this page is a compiled, executed method body - a
test asserts the text is byte-identical to source that javac accepted and that running it reproduces the
recorded answer.

**24 rows are not reproducible by the published recipe at all.**

**10 rows behave differently through the default entry point, 3 of them `LOSSLESS` ones.**
If you use the defaults, these rows do not describe what you will get:

| fixture | classification | required configuration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `nested-array-of-objects-explicit-hints` | `LOSSLESS` | JsonReconstructor.builder().inferArraysFromValues(false).arrayPaths("order_items") |
| `boundary-separator-on-round-trip` | `LOSSLESS` | MapFlattener(true, 50, 1000); JsonReconstructor.builder().separator("__") |
| `vd-preserve-nulls-false-erases-present-null` | `ACCEPTED_LOSS` | JsonReconstructor.builder().preserveNulls(false); probe asserts the default run DIFFERS |
| `vd-comma-format-scalar-with-comma` | `DEFECT` | arrayFormat COMMA_SEPARATED on both sides |
| `vd-comma-format-atomic-coercion` | `DEFECT` | arrayFormat COMMA_SEPARATED on both sides |
| `vd-comma-format-empty-and-trailing-null` | `DEFECT` | arrayFormat COMMA_SEPARATED on both sides |

| `top-level-double-sanitization-asymmetry` | `DEFECT` | MapFlattener(true, 50, 1000); JsonReconstructor.builder().separator("__") |

`covers` is what the document is; `what happens` is precisely what the round trip does to it.
`defaults` is `YES` when the row also holds through the default reconstruction entry point.

Declared LOSSLESS for the round trip, with the parse-time integer loss recorded as out of scope. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-number-text-normalization` | JSON | Exponent notation is not preserved, and that is fine - this fixture calibrates the oracle | `ACCEPTED_LOSS` | The three fractional spellings converge on one canonical form; the integer stays an integer. Nothing about the VALUE is lost. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-empty-containers-end-to-end` | BOTH | The empty-container collapse, followed all the way to the reconstructed JSON document | `DEFECT` | Three different authored values arrive as the same null; nonEmpty is untouched. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-preserve-nulls-false-erases-present-null` | BOTH | preserveNulls(false) converts a present null into an absent key, silently voiding the absent-vs-null guarantee | `ACCEPTED_LOSS` | The present key is gone entirely, not nulled. Defensible because it is explicitly opt-in and the sparse-output use case is legitimate; what is not defensible is the silence in the documentation. | JsonReconstructor.builder().preserveNulls(false); probe asserts the default run DIFFERS | NO | NO | - |
| `vd-string-that-looks-like-array` | BOTH | A scalar string whose text resembles a JSON array turns its parent object into an array | `DEFECT` | The string is destroyed, its characters are retyped as integers, and the enclosing object becomes an array of three synthetic objects. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-array-lookalike-fabricates-padding` | BOTH | The same misdetection then FABRICATES values that were never in the input | `DEFECT` | Only c triggers detection but arrayPaths is keyed on the shared prefix, so b is pulled in and its single 7 is replicated into three records. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-real-array-collides-with-array-text` | BOTH | A genuine array and a string containing its text flatten to byte-identical output | `DEFECT` | Flattened output is identical to the string fixture. Both the array nesting and the element grouping are wrong; the correct answer is an object holding an array, not an array of three objects. | defaults; paired flat-map equality against vd-string-that-looks-like-array | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-comma-format-scalar-with-comma` | BOTH | Under COMMA_SEPARATED, a comma inside an ordinary scalar string invents an array out of nothing | `DEFECT` | Flattening does not touch either value; the damage is entirely on the reconstruct side, where the comma splits the name into two array elements and the sibling is padded by repetition. | arrayFormat COMMA_SEPARATED on both sides | NO | NO | - |
| `vd-comma-format-atomic-coercion` | BOTH | Under COMMA_SEPARATED, four of five strings come back as different types | `DEFECT` | Quoting is gone after flattening, so nothing downstream can know these were strings; parseAtomicValue then returns a boolean, a null, an int with leading zeros dropped, a double with the trailing zero gone, and one surviving String. | arrayFormat COMMA_SEPARATED on both sides | NO | NO | - |
| `vd-comma-format-empty-and-trailing-null` | BOTH | Under COMMA_SEPARATED an array loses an element, not just a distinction | `DEFECT` | Two separate failures: empty-string-to-null (accepted and documented) and three elements becoming two (undocumented, and the reason this is DEFECT rather than ACCEPTED_LOSS). | arrayFormat COMMA_SEPARATED on both sides | NO | NO | - |
| `vd-nested-json-string-length-gate` | BOTH | With parseNestedJsonStrings on, an identical value keeps or loses its type depending on its LENGTH | `DEFECT` | shortJson is expanded into structure; longJson is kept verbatim. Neither field round-trips to its input, and they fail in opposite directions from the same authored type. | MapFlattener.builder().parseNestedJsonStrings(true).maxJsonStringLength(20) | YES | NO | - |
| `vd-control-chars-and-long-string` | BOTH | Control characters, escapes, astral-plane text and a long string all survive intact | `LOSSLESS` | Jackson decodes every escape on the way in and re-escapes correctly on the way out; the surrogate pair stays paired. MapFlattener.escapeString is never reached. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-java-native-temporal-and-identity` | MAP | Instant, UUID and an enum arrive as Strings; Character, Short and Float survive - and nothing marks the difference | `DEFECT` | Instant, UUID and an enum constant all leave the library as Strings; Character, Short and Float survive as themselves. Nothing marks the difference, so nothing downstream can tell an erased UUID from a user string that happens to look like one - the same loss vd-integer-past-long already publishes as a DEFECT. This is the first fixture to reach normalizePrimitive's Temporal, Enum and unknown-type branches at all, because every previous MAP source was built by a JSON parser. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-java-date-is-not-a-function-of-its-input` | MAP | The flattened value of a java.util.Date depends on the JVM's default timezone, not only on the Date | `DEFECT` | A java.util.Date is flattened by calling Date.toString(), which formats through TimeZone.getDefault(). The column value is therefore a function of ambient JVM state, not only of the data: two Spark executors in different regions emit different values for the same row. The epoch instant also becomes an unparseable English sentence. The corpus pins the zone for the measurement and asserts the pin is restored; that pin is itself the evidence, because a fixture that could not be pinned would be flaky. | defaults, with the JVM TimeZone pinned to UTC and Locale to en-US for the measurement | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-binary-array-collides-with-array-text` | MAP | A byte[] flattens to the byte-identical text a real array and an array-lookalike string produce | `DEFECT` | A byte[] never reaches normalizePrimitive: it is diverted to the array path, widened element by element and JSON-serialised, producing the bracket-leading text that a genuine array and an array-lookalike string also produce. The parent object is then retyped as an array AND the binary payload is gone, with none of the base64 marking a ByteBuffer receives. This is the collision class reached with no string and no array anywhere in the input - the type Spark hands you for BinaryType. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-object-array-and-set-become-array-text` | MAP | Object[] and a LinkedHashSet are serialized as array text and promote their parent to an array | `DEFECT` | Object[] and a LinkedHashSet are both serialised to array text, both parse back to two elements, and the parent prefix is promoted, so two independent fields are zipped into two synthetic records. These are the last two container types ordinary Java code hands to flatten() that no fixture reached. Set-ness itself is NOT under test - the oracle renders any Collection positionally - and the fixture says so. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text` | MAP | Double.NaN and the string "NaN" flatten to byte-identical output; one round-trips and one does not | `DEFECT` | Three authored Doubles - NaN and both infinities - and three authored Strings of the same text are the same six characters after flattening. The flattened map is byte-identical to vd-string-literal-lookalikes', which is published LOSSLESS, and the pair invariant asserts that equality. JSON has no NaN literal, so this collision was documented in the warning list and unassertable until the typed input hatch existed. | defaults | YES | YES | - |
| `vd-bigdecimal-java-native-scale-loss-and-the-live-flag` | MAP | A real BigDecimal loses its declared scale by default - and preserveBigDecimalPrecision, inert on the JSON stack, is LIVE here | `DEFECT` | A real BigDecimal handed straight to flatten() loses its declared scale under defaults. The probe additionally shows preserveBigDecimalPrecision producing DIFFERENT output on this stack, which is what makes its inertness on the JSON stack (vd-preserve-bigdecimal-flag-inert) a specific defect rather than a general "this option does nothing". requiresNonDefaultConfig is false: the row is measured at defaults and only the probe tunes the flag. | defaults | YES | YES | - |

## 7. Cross-fixture invariants

Some findings are not visible from any single document - each fixture round-trips or fails on its own
terms, and only the relationship between two of them is the defect. These are asserted separately.

| invariant | kind | holds over | statement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pair-array-text-collides-with-real-array` | FLAT_EQUAL | `vd-string-that-looks-like-array` + `vd-real-array-collides-with-array-text` | A scalar string holding the text of an array and a genuine array flatten to byte-identical output. THREE members of the class are byte-identical and two pairs assert it: vd-binary-array-collides-with-array-text reaches the same bytes from a byte[], with no string and no array anywhere in the input, and pair-binary-collides-with-array-text holds that equality. Object[] and Set are in the class only in the weaker sense - they become bracket-leading strings and retype their parent as a list, on their own element values rather than these ones - so vd-object-array-and-set-become-array-text is pinned by its own recording and by no byte-equality pair. At most one of the three byte-identical members can ever round-trip without a wire-format change. This equality is the value-domain analogue of the FlattenedPath key-injectivity proof. |
| `pair-depth-truncation-aliases-a-real-string` | FLAT_EQUAL | `depth-one-over-max` + `depth-overflow-aliases-a-real-string` | A subtree truncated by maxDepth and a genuine user string containing that same JSON text produce the same flattened map. The depth bound output is indistinguishable from ordinary data; a truncation marker would remove the collision, and the day one is added this assertion flips. |
| `pair-array-bound-preserves-type-at-two` | RECON_TYPE_AT_PATH | `array-size-exactly-max` at `r` | At maxArraySize=3 the reconstructed field is still a list. Baseline for the type-flip assertion below. |
| `pair-array-bound-preserves-type-when-truncating` | RECON_TYPE_AT_PATH | `array-size-one-over-max` at `r` | Truncating from 3 elements to 2 loses data but preserves the container type. This is the well-behaved side of the cliff. |
| `pair-array-bound-of-one-flips-the-type` | RECON_TYPE_AT_PATH | `array-size-max-one-collapses-the-type` at `r` | At maxArraySize=1 the same field reconstructs as an OBJECT, not a shorter list. A resource bound has changed the reconstructed schema. Paired with the two assertions above, this names the type flip directly rather than leaving it inside a general inequality. |
| `pair-single-element-array-degrades-to-scalar` | RECON_TYPE_AT_PATH | `single-element-array-at-the-arity-lower-bound` at `r.tags` | With every limit wide open, a one-element array still reconstructs as a scalar string. This isolates the size>1 detection gate from maxArraySize entirely. |
| `pair-binary-collides-with-array-text` | FLAT_EQUAL | `vd-binary-array-collides-with-array-text` + `vd-string-that-looks-like-array` | A byte[] and a string containing array text flatten to byte-identical output. This is the member of the collision class reachable with no string and no array in the input, which is why it cannot be dismissed as a string-parsing quirk. |
| `pair-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text` | FLAT_EQUAL | `vd-nonfinite-double-collides-with-its-text` + `vd-string-literal-lookalikes` | Deliberately pointed at a published-LOSSLESS row: this LOSSLESS row's flattened output is byte-identical to a document that does not round-trip. The day non-finite doubles are tagged, this equality breaks AND the LOSSLESS row's claim that a genuine string "NaN" must not acquire the tag becomes enforceable in both directions. |
| `pair-binary-promotes-parent-to-list` | RECON_TYPE_AT_PATH | `vd-binary-array-collides-with-array-text` at `a` | The parent of a byte[] reconstructs as a LIST. The binary payload is gone and the container type changed; naming the type flip directly is stronger than leaving it inside a general inequality. |

## 8. Where measurement contradicted the designer

Each fixture carries a hand-traced prediction made before it was run. These are the rows where the
prediction was wrong, kept visible rather than quietly corrected. Every disagreement between a
prediction and a published classification must appear here, and every entry here must correspond to a
real disagreement - the corpus asserts that in both directions.

**`vd-signed-zero` -> `LOSSLESS`**

MEASUREMENT OVERRIDES THE PREDICTION. Predicted ACCEPTED_LOSS on the grounds that the JSON integer -0 loses its sign. It does - but at Jackson parse time, before flatten() is called, so it is absent from the baseline as well as from the result and no part of the round trip under test destroys it. The IEEE-754 double -0.0 is preserved end to end and the MAP arm pins it (rendered via Double.toString, so -0.0 and 0.0 stay distinct). Declared LOSSLESS for the round trip, with the parse-time integer loss recorded as out of scope.

**`avro-decimal-bytes-scale-mismatch` -> `ACCEPTED_LOSS`**

MEASUREMENT OVERRIDES THE PREDICTION. Predicted DEFECT on the grounds that reconstruction throws. It does not: Avro's own DecimalConversion normalises scale with RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY, so 12.5 becomes 12.50 exactly and both fields encode correctly. What survives is the exact numeric value at the declared scale; what changes is the Java representation, from Double to the ByteBuffer the schema mandates. That is an accepted representation change, not a fidelity defect. The two residual faults this datum does NOT reach are recorded in the fixture and are unfixtured gaps.

**`avro-enum-accepted-fixed-decimal-erased` -> `DEFECT`**

DELIBERATE CLASSIFICATION CHANGE, not a measurement disagreement. The designer filed this ACCEPTED_LOSS while stating in the same breath that the fixed-decimal half is a DEFECT and should be split out. It cannot be split without changing the fixture count, so the aggregate label must reflect the worse half. Enum-to-string is genuinely accepted: SQL and Spark have no enum type and the symbol text is a faithful projection. Fixed-decimal-to-bare-bytes is not: precision 18 and scale 4 are gone and the eight bytes are uninterpretable by any consumer of the flattened schema.

**`order-line-items-comma-separated` -> `DEFECT`**

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, ACCEPTED_LOSS -> DEFECT, on review of the loss claims. The fixture was filed as an accepted delimiter collision while its own detail said the reconstructor 'fabricates extra rows and duplicates values' and called that not defensible. The measurement is worse than the label: a two-line order reconstructs as FOUR line items, with SKU-312 repeated three times and quantity 8 attached to two lines that were never ordered. Losing the comma inside 'Bolt, hex, M8' is an accepted consequence of asking for a comma-delimited format; inventing two billable order lines is not, and publishing it under a classification whose repair status reads 'not scheduled for repair' would be indefensible. This follows the precedent already set by avro-enum-accepted-fixed-decimal-erased: where a fixture straddles both categories, the aggregate label must reflect the worse half.

**`financial-transaction-huge-minor-units` -> `DEFECT`**

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, ACCEPTED_LOSS -> DEFECT, on review of the loss claims. This row and vd-integer-past-long measure the identical behaviour - a BigInteger past Long.MAX_VALUE is emitted as a quoted string, every digit intact and the JSON type gone - and the corpus was publishing them under different classifications, so the same fact appeared to a consumer as a defect under repair in one family and an accepted design limit in another. The stated rationale, 'exact-but-retyped beats silently-wrong', compares the behaviour to the older implementation that wrapped to a negative number; that is an argument for why it is no longer a catastrophe, not an argument for why it is correct. The manifest text already conceded it was 'still open and worth separate triage'. Aligned with vd-integer-past-long as DEFECT.

**`recipe-diverges-when-the-flattener-is-tuned` -> `ACCEPTED_LOSS`**

PREDICTED LOSSLESS, MEASURED LOSSY. The design reasoned that a subtree truncated by maxDepth round-trips as the JSON text it was truncated to. It does not: the baseline is the ORIGINAL nested object, so a_b comes back as a string where the source had an object, and truncation is lossy by construction. Published ACCEPTED_LOSS to match depth-one-over-max, which is the identical mechanism at a different bound. The row still does the job it was built for - it is the purpose-built NO case for holdsUnderPublishedRecipe - but its LOSS is not an independent finding and the detail says so.

**`enriched-gavro-parity-claim-fails-on-underscores` -> `ACCEPTED_LOSS`**

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS, with the recording unmoved. The fixture's prediction was correct and is left standing: the enriched defaults do not reproduce GAvroSchemaFlattener's names, and every byte of the measurement is unchanged. What changed is the promise. FlattenOptions' javadoc claimed parity FOR THE DEFAULTS; that claim is withdrawn, because meeting it would mean making ESCAPE the resting state and emitting backslashes into names destined to become Avro and SQL identifiers. A documented, deliberate, configure-around-able difference between two flatteners' conventions is an accepted limit, not a defect - and the way round it, FlattenOptions.gAvroParity(), is now real and is measured by the twin row enriched-gavro-parity-factory-matches-gavro-on-underscored-names on the same schema and datum. Kept as an override rather than by rewriting the prediction, following the precedent of order-line-items-comma-separated: where the measurement has not moved and only the judgement has, the disagreement is the honest record. SCOPE, ADDED ON REVIEW: 'configure-around-able' is true of THIS row's shape and is not true in general, and the page used to publish it without the qualifier. gAvroParity() is exact only for record-rooted schemas that avoid four structural divergences no configuration can express: a union with more than one non-null branch, an array of arrays of records, depth past 50, and a non-record root. The first two are now measured - enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-a-multi-branch-union and enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-an-array-of-arrays-of-records - and on both of them a whole subtree collapses to one leaf, so the column GAvro produces is not reachable here under any configuration at all.

**`enriched-gavro-parity-claim-fails-at-array-boundaries` -> `ACCEPTED_LOSS`**

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS, with the recording unmoved, for the same reason as its sibling on underscores and on the second axis of the same withdrawn claim. The enriched defaults mark array boundaries with __ where GAvroSchemaFlattener emits a single _, and they do so on purpose: a visible boundary marker is a useful convention that FlattenedField.arrayBoundaries() sits alongside. The prediction was correct about the measurement and is preserved; the label reflects that the difference is now declared rather than accidental, and that enriched-gavro-parity-factory-matches-gavro-across-an-array-boundary measures the supported way round it. SCOPE, ADDED ON REVIEW: 'configure-around-able' is true of THIS row's shape and is not true in general, and the page used to publish it without the qualifier. gAvroParity() is exact only for record-rooted schemas that avoid four structural divergences no configuration can express: a union with more than one non-null branch, an array of arrays of records, depth past 50, and a non-record root. The first two are now measured - enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-a-multi-branch-union and enriched-gavro-parity-diverges-on-an-array-of-arrays-of-records - and on both of them a whole subtree collapses to one leaf, so the column GAvro produces is not reachable here under any configuration at all.

**`enriched-escape-name-does-not-decode-across-an-array-boundary` -> `ACCEPTED_LOSS`**

DELIBERATE RECLASSIFICATION, DEFECT -> ACCEPTED_LOSS, with the recording unmoved. The phantom empty segment is still there and the fixture still predicts it; what has been withdrawn is NameCollisionPolicy.ESCAPE's claim to be 'lossless and reversible', which described a decoder this package never shipped. The guarantee is narrowed to the one that is true and useful - injectivity - and the rest of the package already said the rendered name must not be parsed (PathSegment's javadoc, FlattenedField.sourcePath(), arrayBoundarySeparator()); this one javadoc sentence was the outlier. A rendering convention that is documented as not-a-structure, with pathSegments() and arrayBoundaries() carrying strictly more than any decoder could recover, is an accepted limit. Building the decoder was rejected on measurement: it is unsound for boundary markers of the form sep+name+sep, it would force a restriction on a free-form documented option, and it would recover less than the structured path already carries. The injectivity half of the same defect was NOT accepted - it was repaired, and enriched-escape-forged-array-boundary-is-refused is the new row that measures it.

## 9. Running the corpus against your own data

The corpus is not a fixed list you have to accept - it is a harness you can point at your own
documents, which is the only way to find out what *your* data loses.

### Run the published corpus

```bash
./mvnw -o test -Dtest=RoundTripFidelityCorpusTest
```

All 156 documents, on every declared stack, plus the cross-fixture invariants and the
control probes. A green run means the library still behaves exactly as this page says - including still
being broken in exactly the ways it says.

### Add one of your own documents

1. Drop a fixture at `src/test/resources/fidelity/<family>/<your-id>.json`. Copy the nearest existing
   file and replace `input`, `title`, `rationale`, `catchesBugClass`, `cannotCatch` and `predicted`.
   Write `predicted` **before** you run anything - a prediction made after the fact measures nothing.
2. Add a matching entry to `src/test/resources/fidelity/manifest.json` and bump the counts. The corpus fails if a fixture
   file exists that no manifest entry claims, or the reverse, so this step cannot be skipped.
3. Record the measured behaviour:
```bash
./mvnw -o test-compile dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile=target/test-cp.txt
java -cp "target/classes;target/test-classes;$(cat target/test-cp.txt)" \
     io.github.pierce.fidelity.FidelityCorpusRecorder src/test/resources/fidelity
```
   The recorder writes only the `expected` block. It never edits the manifest and never decides a
   classification: it prints the fixtures whose measurement disagrees with the manifest and stops.
   Whether a measured loss is `ACCEPTED_LOSS` or `DEFECT` is a judgement a person makes and signs.
4. Compare your prediction with the recording. Where they differ, add a `classificationOverrides`
   entry saying so; the corpus refuses to let a disagreement go unexplained.

### Just check whether one document survives

If you only want a yes/no answer for a document, you do not need a fixture:

```java
Map<String, Object> src  = new ObjectMapper().readValue(json, new TypeReference<>() { });
Map<String, Object> flat = MapFlattener.builder().build().flatten(src);
Map<String, Object> back = JsonReconstructor.quickReconstruct(flat);
boolean survives = back.equals(src);   // Map.equals, not JsonReconstructor.verify
```

Use `Map.equals`, not `JsonReconstructor.verify()`. `verify()` treats String and Number as a compatible
type pair and compares doubles with an absolute tolerance of `1e-6`; wired to that oracle this corpus
reports the 30-digit-integer row and the decimal-precision row as perfect while the data is demonstrably
changed. It is not a fidelity check.

## 10. Regenerating this document

This page is generated. Editing it by hand is pointless - `RoundTripFidelityDocTest` compares it
against a fresh render of the manifest and fails on any difference. Change `src/test/resources/fidelity/manifest.json`,
then:

```bash
./mvnw -o test-compile dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile=target/test-cp.txt
java -cp "target/classes;target/test-classes;$(cat target/test-cp.txt)" \
     io.github.pierce.fidelity.FidelityDocGenerator \
     src/test/resources/fidelity/manifest.json docs/ROUND_TRIP_FIDELITY.md
```
